utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, I think yesterday I promised to give you an opportunity to raise the matter which you just touched upon for a second only at that time. Please make whatever submissions you wish to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, yesterday at transcript page T-22629, lines 6 to 10, asked that we without delay address Your Honours on the issue of Mr. Mladic not being able to endure the five-day sitting schedule for trial and asking for a four-day week. I will take this opportunity to outline our submissions. As Your Honours know, during the Prosecution phase of the trial, we had the expert medical testimony of two medical doctors from Serbia. They described the mental and physical health of Mr. Mladic and diagnosed him with the risk of transient ischemic attack or mini strokes resulting from his mental limitations and stress created by emotional testimony. These transient ischemic attacks, per the doctors, can lead to death. In order to minimise the risk of the same, these doctors recommended a four-day -- four-day sitting week with Wednesday as a day off from trial, a day of rest for General Mladic. Your Honours will recall that -- that the UNDU medical office likewise supported a four-day sitting week with Wednesday as a day of rest. During the very last part of the Prosecution case in-chief, we sat pursuant to the four-day sitting schedule. The UNDU medical office has regularly reported to Your Honours the benefits of that sitting schedule upon Mr. Mladic as -- and his continued -- and has continued to recommend that this same schedule be applied during the Defence case. Your Honours will recall that a team of three doctors was appointed by the Registry to examine Mr. Mladic at the UNDU and this took place on 27th of November 2013. You will recall that one of these doctors, Dr. Sabri El Bana, examined Mr. Mladic on 10th January 2014 and agreed with his colleagues. It is presumed that he meant the Serbian doctors on the issue of transient ischemic attack, because he recommended a four-day trial sitting week, just as they had. Since the Defence case has started, the UNDU medical report filed weekly has repeatedly recommended to the Chamber that the four-day sitting schedule similar to the Prosecution phase of the case be employed during this phase of the case. Thus, Your Honours, we have a total of four medical professionals, two Serbian, and -- engaged by the Defence team, one from UNDU and one independently appointed by the Registry, who are all recommending due to the health of Mr. Mladic that we sit for four days a week instead of five. Now, we are telling that you Mr. Mladic himself expresses his fatigue and ill effects on his health from having the five-day schedule, thus far imposed during the Defence case in-chief. Mr. Mladic would like to add that it is his understanding that many other accused had four-day sitting schedules who do not even have the medical impairments that he suffers from, such as Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Karadzic, and in the case of Mr. Prlic et al. Mr. Mladic feels he is being treated unequally in relation to these other accused. Accordingly, based on the medical professionals who have stated on paper that we should be sitting four days a week with Wednesday as a rest day, we would ask Your Honours to give due deference to these doctors' opinions and schedule four days of trial a week with Wednesday as a day of rest to provide benefit to Mr. Mladic for his medical impairments. That was all we had, Your Honours. Thank you for the opportunity to address this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Groome, do you want to respond and do you want to do it now or would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll make some submissions now, Your Honour. But before I do, can I just inquire of Mr. Lukic: Several weeks ago I had the impression that there were additional experts being brought in by the Defence to do additional examinations of Mr. Mladic, could I have an update of that? Is there something pending or are there additional reports we can view?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is really pending. Those doctors never appeared and we are still waiting for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So in that case, Your Honour, the Prosecution's response or submissions regarding this request is as follows. Any unnecessary delays to the trial should be avoided. I think the victims of the crimes and the international community have an important interest in the expeditious conclusion of this trial. It is the Prosecution's submission that in order for the Chamber to grant the request of the Defence, the Chamber must find that shortening the work week is medically necessary. In turn for the Chamber to find that a reduction is medically necessary, two criteria must be met. First that medical personnel directly responsible for the care of the accused or engaged as experts to evaluate his health are of the opinion that a shortened week is medically necessary. I note in this regard the current opinion of the medical staff of the UNDU that a four-day court schedule will be generally beneficial to Mr. Mladic's health. The Prosecution submits that the fact that his health would generally benefit from a shortened work week is insufficient to establish that a reduction of the work week is medically necessary. I am sure that each of our physicians would say that our general health would be improved by an additional day devoted to rest and relaxation. Second, any medical recommendation for a shortened work week should be based on objectively observable criteria. As far as the medical information that we regularly receive, General Mladic's values for key indicators of health have consistently been within normal range and his treatment plan has remained unchanged for quite some time now. Absent any evidence to the contrary or evidence of -- absent any evidence of abnormalities, there is no basis for reducing the working schedule. Finally while the Chamber's determination of this request must be made on factors directly related to Mladic's health and its impact on trial proceedings, it is not unrelated to the way in which the Defence case is being conducted. We are now a month into the Defence case, and I think it is a fair observation that a substantial part of the Defence case to date consists of evidence which is clearly tu quoque. It is also I think fair to say that tu quoque evidence is that is being led by the Defence probably consumes a day or more of each week's work. Some witnesses offer little more than tu quoque evidence. For example, out of the 29 paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, there may be a technical problem. Is there a technical problem, Mr. Stojanovic? Could you please consult with Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just heard from my colleague that there is no B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll -- I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's been solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, it's at least I receive B/C/S translation if I move to channel 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I suggest that we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was speaking about the example of Dragan Lalovic. Out of the 29 paragraphs in his 92 ter evidence, only two had direct bearing on this case. Much was in exposition of his military career and events that can only be characterised as tu quoque. Last week a substantial amount of time was spent trying to understand with precision the evidence of the protected witnesses regarding how many severed heads he alleged were hung from a church door and how many he alleged were tied around the necks of dogs. While I appreciate the Chamber has an obligation to ensure that any evidence that is adduced is both clear and precise, I was unable to discern how this evidence would ultimately assist the Chamber in its determination of the charges in the indictment. So to return to the issue of the Defence's request for a shortened work week, I ask the Defence to re-evaluate the time it is taking adducing evidence that is purely tu quoque. For our part, the Prosecution will now be more consistent in raising objection to such evidence in both this written and oral forms. I ask the Court to reflect on the amount of time spent on such issues and whether such will ultimately be germane to its deliberations, and if not then to exercise its oversight of proceedings in a way that minimise's the time spent on such matters. At least then if we reach a stage when a reduced work week becomes medically necessary, it will have less impact on the overall length of the trial and the prospect of justice for victims of these crimes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, in your response you have not addressed the inequality raised by Mr. Lukic comparing the situation of Mr. Mladic with Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Tolimir, and Mr. Prlic and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know the specific circumstances of those cases and what -- what was the basis of those Chambers' deciding that the interests of justice required four-day work weeks. If the Chamber would like us to investigate that and would like submissions on that, but I -- I suggest that the -- the -- the determination is more properly made on this Chamber's assessment of the factors that it is aware of and that the determination should not be based upon a superficial comparison with -- with what other Chambers have decided with respect to what the interests of justice required in those trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Lukic, do you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- reply --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just briefly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My learned friend raised the issue of necessary medical -- medically necessary test. We think it is medically necessary somebody can die because of a -- fatigue. We think it's medically necessary enough to show that, and it's obviously shown in previous reports. In regard of tu quoque Defence, I would strongly disagree with my colleague that we brought witnesses that are tu quoque witnesses. The fact is that Dragan Lalovic was the witness who was actually testifying about the period before the war, so he did not have much to say about the -- the -- our -- our indictment but doesn't mean that it's not necessary to show the period that led to the war. And we have to see the full picture. If we watch a box match and we can see only one boxer, it's senseless if he just waves his hands if the other boxer is invisible. We have to see the other boxer to see the boxing match to see the real situation, so we have to show the situation on the ground. Showing only one side will not help this Court to understand that period of time in Bosnia-Herzegovina and to understand the war and to understand what happened because of that war if we watch only one side. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. The Chamber will consider the request and we'll also consider whether we need further submissions or whether we'll decide on the request on the basis of what has been presented until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will also consider at what point in time we'll decide on the motion and whether we'll wait for the outcome of the examination that took place yesterday. I don't know exactly when to expect a report, but we'll further inquire into that. Then I think we are at the point where we could have the witness in so as to continue his cross-examination. Mr. Usher. It also gives me an opportunity to deal with the following matter. On the 3rd of June of this year, the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D3239 was assigned Exhibit D505 and marked for identification due to its not being accompanied by a B/C/S translation. On the 11th of June, the Defence informed the Chamber and the Prosecution that the B/C/S translation of the document in question has been uploaded into e-court under document ID 1D09-2433. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the B/C/S translation to D505 and admits the exhibit into evidence. If there are any further questions about the translation, then, of course, the Chamber would like to hear from the Prosecution within the next two working days. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Just to inquire whether VWS was able to retrieve a statement from the witness yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it has been provided to the Chamber and a copy will be provided to the parties. But it is, as far as we could see, it's one of the two other statements. Most likely the one -- the 25-paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me be careful. Let me see whether it's -- it's -- yes. It's a 25-paragraph statement which very much resembles, apart from one or two handwritten short notes in B/C/S, which very much resembles what we've seen before. But you'll be provided with a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Batinic. We'll continue. I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Ms. Hasan will now continue her cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Batinic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now we've seen the notes that you provided to the Chamber yesterday. These are the notes that you said Mr. Lukic gave you. Could you please tell us when that was? When were you given those documents?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that those notes were given by Mr. Lukic. It was Mr. Dundjer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's make sure we're talking about the same thing. I'm talking about the list of questions on which you had put some handwritten notes. Were those provided to you by Mr. Dundjer or Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now I know what this is all about. This is the list. However, yesterday I provided another list as well to the driver of this Tribunal so that he could bring that to you. Hence, the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the -- I take it that's the -- the statement he had kept which Madam Registrar will provide you a copy of.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So the -- the ones that we're talking about, the list of questions you have before you, when were those given to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list of questions, I think it was two days ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And who was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes. Was anyone else present?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just me and Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday at transcript page 22602, lines 4 to 5, Judge Orie asked you a question about that list. And he asked you whether there were only questions or if there were hints to answers or any other notes. And you responded: "No, it's simply questions," and that had you made some notes?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could call up 65 ter 30803.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, it's possible that the Chamber didn't translate your notes based on the answer you gave, but we have translated those into English and that's what he you're going to see now. Now, under the heading "Armament," it will come up in a moment, and I can see you have your hard copy in front of you, just on the first page of your notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the wrong page, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's the wrong B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On the right side of the screen, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We have the right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- totally different.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry. Yeah, the right side of the screen should be the English. If we can go to the next page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Under the heading "Armament," about -- little under -- little below halfway down that page, there's a question there and it says: "What did people feel at the time [sic]?" Do you see that, sir? It's at the bottom of the B/C/S page. And we can see next to that you've -- I take it those are your handwritten notes where you've written fear and uncertainty, helplessness, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could turn to the second B/C/S page, please. Now, Witness, at the top of that page and just below the question, there's some typed text there. And as I read it, it says: "Uncertainty, fear, helplessness." Mr. Batinic, those are not your notes, are they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are my note, Your Honours. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think -- let's try to see exactly what we are talking about. What we are looking at at this moment specifically, Witness, is what you see on your screen to be type written on the first line of this page. There are three words. I don't know how to pronounce them but "Neizvesnost," "Strah," "Bespomocaost"; these words. Are these your notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything that is typewritten are Mr. Lukic's questions. And the handwritten notes were my notes that I made in the hotel as a reminder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Statement 65 ter 30798 uploaded by the Prosecution, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. What's -- let me just -- one second. One second, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is from his statement. It's not my notes. You can see paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all there were overlapping speakers so, therefore, we have not -- The witness has answered the question saying that everything that's handwritten are his notes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and that everything which is type written is what was provided to him as he told us by you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Those are his words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those notes made by me were his words and we can find it at paragraph 5 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, his statement is not in evidence so the Chamber doesn't know that. You can, of course, in re-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you can deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to draw your attention, Your Honours, that these are his words not mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if they are in his statement, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we know something about how this statement -- this was -- and that's the issue, and you should have refrained -- stayed out of it. The simple question was whether these were notes provided to him irrespective of whether at an earlier stage he may have used this and that's a different matter. That's argumentive. It has got nothing to do with the question. Therefore, please explore the matter any further in re-examination if you wish to do so. And Ms. Hasan may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, Witness, what you told the Chamber yesterday that these were only questions wasn't true, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer in the following way. Now I have a clear picture. These are words from my statement that Mr. Lukic typed up and I took that to the hotel, and then I added my notes just as a reminder for myself so that I wouldn't is skip anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what now happens may - I'm saying may - well demonstrate why you should have stayed out of -- you should have not have intervened in the cross-examination. Let that be clear to you and remind that very well if you intervene again. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: At this stage I'd offer 65 ter 30803 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? Not. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30803 receives number P6593, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, you're not a ballistics expert, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I'm not a ballistics expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You have no expertise in crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No expertise but I have personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Have you undergone any training as respect to mortars and their impacts?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any experience with mortars, but I had experience with mortar shells that fell all around me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Have you ever fired a mortar yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you mentioned, sir, that you were a history teacher. Can you tell us what level you taught?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a history teacher, which means I'm qualified to teach secondary school. In 1986 and 1987, I also worked in an elementary school. And then I landed a job at the Vrace memorial park from the Second World War where I worked as a curator. And there were also three other museums around Sarajevo which I also dealt with and was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And your employment as an elementary school teacher up until the start of the war, all your employment was in the Igman area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I worked in Hadzici at that time, a small place near mount of Igman. And during the war I saw my students, my former students in positions on Mount Igman. They were already grown up men by then.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And before the war you also lived in the Igman area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived at the Mostar junction. I have a house there. It is 7 kilometres away from Mount Igman, and from my house there's a very good view of Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And this is where you lived also during the war. Is this in the Kovacevic area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I got married in 1985, I stayed living there with my wife; whereas, my parents lived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, in June of 1992 when you were mobilised, what brigade were you mobilised into?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were attached to the Igman Brigade. But if we're talking about mobilisation, I didn't even see the Igman Brigade at the time. People came to the village who were members of the Igman Brigade. They mobilised us and they sent us to positions. Before that I was a -- a member of the village guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in June of 1992 when this happened, was the brigade known by any other name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what are we talking about? What happened in 1992? Can you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, when you were mobilised and you said you were attached to the Igman Brigade, was it actually the Igman Brigade at that time? Was it not the Blazuj Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. When we were mobilised, we were taken to the position in Zenik which is some 10 kilometres away from Blazuj.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir, but I'm simply asking you which brigade you were attached to. Is your answer that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, at that time I didn't have any personal contacts with the Igman Brigades or the Blazuj Brigade, as you call it. Perhaps it was renamed later but I wouldn't know that. My first contact with the Igman Brigade was on the 29th of June. That's when I went there in order to repair my jammed machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. And who was the commander of the brigade that you were attached to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was their interpreter, the commander was Captain Blagota Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to put it to you that it's actually Blagoje Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't agree with you. Perhaps that's what you can find in documents. However, I was in -- his interpreter for three months and he always introduced himself as Blagota, and he always said that in the documents his name is Blagoje. For example, in my ID my date of birth is the 13th of February, although my mother told me that I was born on the 12th of February. His name is Blagota. He is currently retired --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you consider this to be two different persons or two different ways of spelling or writing his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's one and the same person, Your Honours. Blagota and Blagoje is one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the issue seems to be rather futile. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what was his rank?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain. Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday we -- you gave some testimony about the bread line massacre incident, and this was on the Vasin Miskina Street. So I'd like to ask you just if you can tell us, the Vasin Miskina Street, it's in the far east of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I said that it was a massacre. Second of all, Vase Miskina Street is in the very centre of Sarajevo, in the old part of the Austro-Hungarian city of Sarajevo, very close to the eternal fire. The main street is Marsala Tito Street and Vase Miskina was a street off it. Today its name is Ferhadija.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I don't think we disagree that it's in the old town of Sarajevo. Now where did this meeting, that you say took place in 1993, where did that take place?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, the commander was Colonel Spasoje Cojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, I asked you where the meeting took place in 1993 that you attended about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meeting was held in the -- the office of the brigade commander of the Igman Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And isn't Igman about -- over 15 kilometres or so from the Vase Miskina Street?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. I know that my house is 15 kilometres away. There's another kilometre to Blazuj. So it's up to 17 kilometres at the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And this incident that took place in fact then was nowhere near the zone of responsibility of the Igman Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That incident had nothing to do with the Igman Brigade, and it was not close to it. The point is that the commander who was an artillery man explained to the military observers as to what had happened, and I was there as an interpreter who interpreted for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were not yourself involved in the investigation of this incident, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I was just an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you never saw the pathologist report that the commander was basing his conclusions on, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't see that report. The commander never showed it to me. May I be allowed to add something, please? I read General McKenzie's book about the incident --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no need to say anything about what General McKenzie may have written. Next question please, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I take it then that did you not see this pathologist report after the meeting? Until this day, you haven't seen it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I have not seen it. Why would I need to look at the pathologist's report? There's no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So really, Mr. Batinic, all you're telling us basically that the extent of your knowledge is simply what Commander Cojic told you in 1993, one year after this incident took place, about what he personally thought caused the casualties on the Vase Miskina Street?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander told them, the military observers. And I was just an interpreter who interpreted for him when he spoke about the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So if I ask you, sir, whether you give any credence to what Commander Cojic said to those foreign observers that day, do you? Do you give credence to what he said? That this was a staged event caused by claymore mines?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to explain the situation in some detail? I was intrigued by the event --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and there are some things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that I wanted to check in 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. What you were asked, and you're invited to answer the question, is whether you give any credence to what Commander Cojic said; namely, that it was a staged event.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are some elements that I fully believed and gave credence to, which is why I thought that the commander was right. May I be allowed to explain now?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm just going to go on with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could take a look at 65 ter 30781, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, as you can see here, sir, this is photo documentation that formed part of the police investigation file into this incident on the Vase Miskina Street on the 27th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to page 2 of the B/C/S, please. That's just the cover page of the photo file. And now can we turn to page 6. Now these are just photographs. We can just look at the B/C/S document. And if I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the Chamber has already heard evidence about patterns that are created or left by mortars and artillery. They've heard about this in this case. Now, Cojic said that these casualties resulted from claymore mines that were planted in basements, so what I'd like you to do is please explain for us is how claymore mines create patterns like this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a ballistics expert so I can't explain the traces. However, with your leave I could explain or tell you about what Cojic said. We went to the spot with SAS and the British service and we examined the place. This is a police report and I can't comment on, but I can comment upon what I heard and what I saw with other people who are much better versed in such matters. They were members of the special British forces, SAS.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, Witness, what you heard others say or what others think about this is not what I'm interested in at the moment. I just simply want to know whether you have an explanation as to -- because you said you give some credence to what Commander Cojic said, whether you can explain this to us and evidently you cannot. What I'd --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I can. This is precisely what I wanted to tell you some ten minutes ago. If I may be allowed to explain, I will gladly do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation for how claymore mines create craters like this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Asked and answered. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has no explanation from what I understand. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I simply asked the question because the witness on line 3 says: "This is precisely what I wanted to tell you some ten minutes ago," but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- appreciate he can -- he said before that he can't answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you wanted to explain is not about what you see on the screen at this moment is it, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd offer 65 ter 30781 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If this is accepted, we'll have to employ our expert witnesses to explain this incident as well, and we will gladly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The Defence can choose to call whoever they want. I -- I don't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because incident is not in our indictment. But if it's accepted as an exhibit, we'll have to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if it's not in the indictment why did you then deal with it in examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness told us. What he told us, we reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you -- whatever a witness says, relevant, irrelevant, you just record it and say put it here and then blame the Prosecution for taking proper notice of it and paying attention to it, or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we are allowed to elaborate on this incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- we do not have objection for this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- document to enter into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact what happened, Mr. Lukic, is that you bring a witness who has no personal knowledge whatsoever about an event but whatever he heard someone else say, matters which require expertise, I would agree with you, that you put that before the Chamber highly suggesting that there is some truth in the explanation given by what this witness heard. And then don't be surprised if the Prosecution then responds to that by saying, "But there is a report about it." You haven't provided, as far as I can see, any supporting documentary material. You just bring in what this witness heard, apparently not concerned about what the basis of his knowledge is. If you would say the only reason why we presented this evidence is because we want to tell the Chamber what this witness heard someone else to say, then I would say book your agenda until 2020, because then we'll not yet ready with this case. I think you're blaming the Prosecution for something you triggered yourself, and we'll consider whether or not we'll give it some more thought. If you want to further make submissions on your objections to admission, please do so at this moment. If it was what you said, then we'll give Ms. Hasan an opportunity to respond and finally we'll decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you want to add anything to your objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just said that we will then have to deal with the incident as -- in the whole with [Overlapping speakers] witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Hasan, well, you respond already that the Defence can proceed as it deems fit. Is that your response?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's -- that's correct, Your Honour has understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I already said then we do not have any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will -- it will be marked for identification. The Chamber will consider --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were on your feet. Was that to put your next question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I just wanted to address the admission of this -- of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: As you've already stated, it -- you know, this was raised by the Defence in their 65 ter notice. It even says -- it goes further and says the witness will testify about an incident at the bread queue in Sarajevo that had been blamed on the Serbs but was actually the result of claymore mines planted by the ABiH. So we can only go off what the Defence is telling us, is putting us on notice of, so this goes directly to the credibility of this witness who is giving the Chamber evidence about an incident that took place. If the -- if the Defence wants to withdraw this part of the witness's evidence on this incident, then I can withdraw the admission -- our offer to admit this into evidence. But if they maintain that evidence, then this certainly should go in as it contradicts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it is clear that you tendered this document not for the purposes of establishing how the incident happened but exclusively to -- for testing the credibility and the reliability of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Both, Your Honour. For both purposes. The -- the -- the evidence about this -- this is the not the first time that this incident comes in this trial. In fact, the ballistics report is already in evidence in this case. So this certainly adds to that. And I think it goes in for both purposes, the credibility and for its contents, for what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, anything to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that it's good for us to sit after the trial, me and Ms. Hasan, to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would say after this hearing. Yes. After the trial might be a bit late.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the hearing. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's understood. If you would sit together, the document will be marked for identification for the time being. And Madam Registrar, it would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30781 receives number P6594, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6594 is marked for identification. We are at a time for a break, Ms. Hasan. Mr. Batinic, we take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after the break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just ask Ms. Hasan or Mrs. Hasan? Could I please be present during that coffee with Mr. Lukic. I would be pleased for all of us to meet up. So I would like to be present, simply to be there with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, both parties are not allowed to even have contact with the witness once he has taken the stand, but I hope you'll enjoy, nevertheless, your coffee on your own. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Lukic, I'm also specifically asking your attention. When the witness was about to leave the courtroom, both Judge Moloto and I even could hear Mr. Mladic say something aloud, including the name of counsel for the Prosecution. That's totally inappropriate. No communication with whomever in this courtroom, especially not if the name of a counsel of the Prosecution is part of that. Therefore, if this kind of things happens again, and it happened a couple of times over the last week, this is the last warning. And especially if it is not just to say something but including a name of someone who plays a role in this proceedings, and if the Chamber can't hear that, apart from hearing that name, then we'll take action. Let that be clear for Mr. Mladic. We now continue. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. At the same time, there was a problem with the B/C/S -- with the translation of P6593. Madam Registrar, do I understand that a new translation has been uploaded?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was a problem with both English and B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- with the order of the pages, so new version of both B/C/S and English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- is uploaded with a new number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that, I understand, has been uploaded under 65 ter number 30803a. Therefore, you are hereby instructed to replace the document which is now known under P6593 by the one I just mentioned. Ms. Hasan, you're on your feet. Anything before the witness comes in or?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I was just waiting for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I inquire with the parties whether the document that was provided by the witness and given to you, a copy this morning, that -- can the original be returned to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We received a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, also no reason to keep the original?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, Ms. Hasan will now continue her cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, you've told us that you spent quite a bit of time with the UNMOs. And am I correct that you were interpreting for them throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. A lot of time. Actually, from the end of June 1992 I interpreted for the UNMOs on the Serb side, and later on I was interpreting for the other parties in the conflict, other commanders; for example, in Gorazde at that time Buljubasic was -- on the Muslim side was commander there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Turning your mind to July 1993, do you recall interpreting for Lieutenant-Colonel John Hamill?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We became great friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, on the 20th of July, 1993, you were accompanying him to Poljine to pay someone for damages that had been caused to their vehicle in November of 1992. Now, I'm not interested in that specific trip but I just want to ask you if you recall being with Mr. John Hamill on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that full well. It doesn't have to do damage on his vehicle. It has to do with damage to a vehicle of a civilian who lived up there in Poljine, Mrkovici, I think, and Chris Hansen [phoen], a Norwegian captain, was with us too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now you were still with -- together with the UNMOs in the following days, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the time. Until the Dayton Accords were signed in 1995, I was with UN Observers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, in that case you surely period about the bombardment of Sarajevo by the Serbs that took place over the next two days?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember that was discussed quite a bit, and John Hamill talked about it as well. There was quite a bit of shelling. I don't know exactly what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, let's -- let's look at what Lieutenant-Colonel John Hamill said about that. And this was just two days after your trip with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So if I can call up Exhibit P00537.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, it's common practice that first questions are put to the witness before any statement or anything else is put to him. Now, I do not know what your questions will be, but could you please keep that in the back of your mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: My -- my question leading up to this was whether he heard about it, and his answer was he heard -- he heard about quite some -- that there was some shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And ... if -- if that -- if there are any details in what Hamill would have said you could elicit from the witness first without showing him the testimony of Mr. Hamill, then I think that would be preferable. And if there's any contradiction, then of course you could still put to the witness what Mr. Hamill said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, Witness, you -- you said there quite a bit of shelling happening and can you tell me what you mean by "quite a bit of shelling"? What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which event you're referring to, which day? I mean, all these things that were happening. But as far as shelling is concerned from any side, military observers were divided into two sections. They communicated on Motorolas. One side was called Papa and one side was called Lima. The Lima side was the Serb side and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you were not asked all this. You -- Ms. Hasan introduced a matter as the two days following your trip with Mr. Hamill about some damages. And she asked when you said there was quite a bit of shelling to further explain that. Not to explain the monitoring system but what you experienced in terms of shelling those two days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Honourable Prosecutor, the shelling itself I don't know what it has to do with. There was practically shelling every day. Could you please be specific in your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. So do you recall that in the day and -- or two after the 20th of July, so the 21st and 22nd of July, that there was one of the heaviest days of bombardment of the city of Sarajevo by the Bosnian Serbs when 3.600 rounds fell into the city? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the shelling of the city, but the date, when, what was shelled, and when I was exactly with John Hamill, I was with him many times, so I don't know what this pertains to specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So let's just be clear. Do you remember that there was 3.600 shells falling on the city of Sarajevo, a huge bombardment of the city, in and around that time? Does that stand out in your mind.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. I know that there was shelling of the city, but we were on the Serb side. How can I now speak about the shelling of the city when our only communication with the other side is with the observers on the other side via Motorola?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at what the -- the UNMOs that, you know, you were working with wrote about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could see Exhibit P00540, please. And this is a report on the events between 21 July and 22 July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, sir, if you look at -- I guess you can take your pick, the English or the B/C/S, it says under item 1A: "The situation has changed absolutely since yesterday (midnight). Sarajevo has been heavily shelled: Into the down-town were recorded 680 impacts, and UNMOs observed a total of 3.777 outgoing rounds from the Serbian weapons positions." And it goes on to say, and this goes over on the B/C/S page too, that seven people were killed and 49 were wounded as a result. Witness, did you hear the UNMOs talking about this? Did you hear about this heavy shelling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have the English on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we were on the --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It seems we've lost the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we were on the first page of the English version where the seven deaths were mentioned. Yes, there we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I just want to know. You were there. You were with these UNMOs. You were -- you've told us about the -- the attacks on the Serbs in Sarajevo, and you've told us about that at length. So I'm asking you about whether this bombardment, whether you heard about this, whether you experienced this? Because you were with them.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the shelling itself in this document, I have no doubt, as far as this document is concerned, and I have no right to doubt it. It is a document of the military observers. I just want to simplify the situation. The military observers were in two zones, the Papa zone and the Lima zone, and that is very important in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This report is about outgoing shells, large numbers. So you don't have to explain that. You said it was discussed quite a bit. What was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I can say to Your Honour is that via Motorola the reports of the other side could be heard, about the shells being fired. But how many there were, I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently you being able to hear conversations on the Motorolas, with Motorolas, did you experience that there was heavy, heavy, heavy shelling? I mean, it's described that the situation changed entirely; that is, that the shelling was far more intense than usual.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that. I could only follow this with John --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You believe that. What do you mean by "believe"? I'm asking you whether you observed that the shelling was far more intense than usual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that there was fighting. I know that there was a battle going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you for an explanation why there may have been more shelling. I'm asking you whether you observed the shelling to be more intense than usual on that day or the two days following the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. There was more shelling, and the reports were sent via Motorola all the time, and John was receiving them. Yes, that is correct. There was heavy shelling. But let me say that I cannot say exactly how many shells there were and it's not my job. That's what the military observers know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one asked you. It was put to you that 3.600 or perhaps even 3.700 shells fell. And where you say there was shelling every day, if this was more intense, then a reference to shelling that took place every day where it was far more intense these days is evasive, is not the whole truth. Would you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was more intensive shelling. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then a reference to shelling was there every day is really evasive. Ms. Hasan, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, Witness, that was in July of 1993. Let's go to June, one month before that; June of 1993, okay? So there's evidence in this case that there was shells falling into the city of Sarajevo at a rate of about 1.000 shells per day. Did you hear any reports of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any report, especially not written ones, and I did not have any front of me. How can I know about the written reports of military observers? I was a field interpreter. I did not translate any reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you heard any reports that day. The question was not whether you translated written reports but whether you heard any reports of a thousand shells a day. That was the question. Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm going ask you, then, about the conditions in Sarajevo around that time. Let's talk about July, June/July of 1993. There were days when the city was -- many days when the city was without electricity. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you hear about citizens having to go to wells to get their water supplies and that there was a huge demand for water that was not available. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw that on television. Yes, I heard about that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what about the targeting of UN observation posts? The UNMOs reported about UN observation posts being attacked by the Serbs. Did you hear about those attacks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you explain that word that you used, that "post" of the UN observers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: These were observation posts. Did you hear about the targeting of, for example, OP-Papa 5 and OP-Papa 4 in 1993, early 1993? Did you hear about the Bosnian Serbs attacking those observation posts?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about the shelling of observation posts. Again, we heard the other side. They were leaving these posts panic-stricken. Papa 4, Papa 5, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just going to move onto another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just -- you said: "Again, we heard the other side." What did you mean exactly by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tried to explain that. There are two observation missions at the headquarters in Sarajevo. One is on the Serb side and the other is on the Muslim side. Papa is on the Bosnian side, Lima is the one that's on the Serb side. That is to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- they are the ones that we -- or rather they communicated via Motorola. They communicated. And that is how we hear these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- that's clear, because your answer was -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's what I wanted to explain at the very outset so that there wouldn't be any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, if we can take a look at 65 ter 30792. Now, you've told us you did hear about the attacks on the -- the observation posts. This is a -- what you'll see is an UNPROFOR sitrep. Now, under the general situation under item 1, it talks about these attacks and it reports on the targeting of OPs and then it goes on to say -- sorry. It says: "Papa 4 and 5 were targeted today with some harassing rounds falling within 50 metres of the positions. However, it was neither prolonged nor intense. In view of the frequent shelling" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Please slow down when reading, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, you heard the admonishment to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: "In view of the frequent shelling of the Papa OPs, I will ask for a meeting with the commander in Lukavica to hopefully put a stop to these occurrences." Now, it goes on to say: "Lima side UNMOs were called to the Blazuj hospital to witness that two of the oxygen bottles delivered by the UNHCR were found to contain gunpowder. Once confirmed, this matter was turned over to CIVPOL." Witness, is this the incident you talked about yesterday at the Blazuj hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that this is the same incident. I mentioned only two bottles, but as far as I remember there were ten of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, despite your certainty which you testified about yesterday at transcript page 22625, your certainty that this happened in 1992, October or November, we see here that this report is dated the 24th of January, 1993. Do you dispute the accuracy of this report in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may object at this moment. This evidence is in contradiction with the evidence we saw on that video. Here, it's noted that two bottles actually were filled with gunpowder. There, we saw one bottle with gunpowder and the other bottle with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- mortar fuses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So -- well, it's not an objection, I think, to the question. It's a matter to be further explored, which you could do, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I fully agree with you, in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The evidence wrongly presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The evidence yesterday was about two bottles of oxygen. To that extent you're right, Mr. Lukic. One filled with gunpowder and the other one with mortar fuses. Ms. Hasan, that was the evidence of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, do you -- I'll move onto another document that will help with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can we turn to 65 ter 30794.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, you earlier said there were ten bottles. Now the evidence of yesterday says there were two bottles, found, oxygen bottles, with -- one with gunpowder, the other one with mortar fuses, out of five. So I don't know where the ten now comes from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we just did not receive interpretation for a while. Everything that you said just now had not been interpreted. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what General Mladic said now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we check whether Mr. Mladic now receives interpretation. At least I receive interpretation on channel 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it can be heard, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll resume. I said: "Mr. Batinic, you earlier said that there were ten bottles. Now the evidence of yesterday says there were two bottles found, oxygen bottles, one with gunpowder, the other one with mortar fuses, out of five, so I don't know where the ten now comes from." And that was my question to Mr. Batinic. You said there were ten. Yesterday we heard about five. Out of those five, two were filled with contraband. Could you tell us where the ten come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I still claim it's ten bottles. Because I and the military observers entered the storage room of the hospital and that's where we opened the first bottle. And I said that the gunpowder became an emulsion when contacting water. After that, French UNPROFOR people came with an interpreter, as far as I can see, and also local TV --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and then in front of them bottles were opened, as we saw yesterday, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we saw on television that out of five two were containing -- it's still not explained yet where the ten comes from. I know now a lot of other things but my question has not been truly answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see ten bottles in the storage with my own two eyes when I arrived there with the observers. There were ten bottles in the storage. Later on, people came and opened the other bottles in front of a TV crew. I'm talking about the hospital storage or storeroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the other bottles, other than the two that we saw being opened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those other bottles remained in the hospital store room. That's a fact. They were not taken out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But whether they contained any contraband or whether they were just as the other three out of the five were just filled with oxygen, do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to Dr. Pejic who was the chief administer, there were ten bottles. Some had already been opened. An employee even tried to heat one of the bottles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you again. You say there were ten bottles. Were there ten bottles found to be filled with contraband; gunpowder, whatever? Anything else than oxygen? Or was it just the two that were found to be filled with contraband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I only know that in this case shall we're talking about three bottles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, if -- yes. I take it that a hospital will have more oxygen bottles. That's -- so the ten is irrelevant at this moment. Ms. Hasan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This is a sitrep for the 26th of January, 1993. Okay? Now, if we turn to the English, page 2, in the B/C/S page 3, we have a report here on some oxygen cylinders that the UNMOs were called in to have a look at, and they write here in their report first full paragraph: "During inquiry, it came to light that the Serbian claimed to have stolen five oxygen cylinder from the UNHCR truck two months ago." Now it goes onto describe that: "After using three cylinder, they got near about 160 fuse for mortar shells from one of those cylinders and a huge quantity of gunpowder from the other cylinder. All the fuses were separately wrapped in an old invoice copies from a company in Visoko. The invoice were all dated 1986. The Serbian press were present and filmed the proceeding. After visit to that hospital (Blazuj) we went straight to Kosevo Hospital to verify the number of oxygen cylinder in their stock. But nothing unusual was noticed." Now, Witness, it certainly contradicts -- is not consistent with some of the evidence you've given today and yesterday about this event. Is this, in fact, did you learn the same thing that the UNMOs report here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know nor did I know what the UN observers' report contained. As far as my statement is concerned, I was not precise. I didn't say the exact time. It was in 1992, the beginning of January. It was rather warm. I was in a light blue jacket. That's why I assumed it was the end of January. But there's no doubt that we're talking about the same people, the same containers. The footage shows that. What happened at the check-point where those bottles had been confiscated, I really don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd offer 65 ter 30794 as well as 65 ter 30792 into evidence, the two sitreps. THE COURT REPORTER: Can you say that number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, 65 ter 30792.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30792 receives number P6595. And document 30794 receives number P6596, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6595 and P6596 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you testified about Mr. Guzina in relation to the hostages. Did you see Mr. Svetozar Guzina here in The Hague before you testified?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Mr. Guzina. He is my friend. We had a drink together, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you discuss any of the evidence he was to give or you were to give?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not discuss his evidence at all. I know I don't have the right to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me be a bit more precise. Did you discuss with Mr. Guzina his involvement with these hostages?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not discuss hostages or that crisis. We discussed many other things, Mr. Guzina and I. We hadn't seen each other perhaps for a whole year.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So this evidence about Guzina's involvement with the hostages, did you tell the Defence about that before you testified?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say anything to the Defence about Mr. Guzina's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, the UNMOs that were -- that were held and that you were with in 1995, they were held in Blazuj; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And to be more precise, it was 1 kilometre west of Blazuj at the Mostar junction.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, who kept them there? Who held them there? Was it the Igman Brigade or the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Igman Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move onto your testimony about the Markale market massacre, and that was February 5th, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, sorry, I'm just going to have to go back because the record records you as having asked a question. This is at, if you look at your screen, page 42, line 7. I asked you who kept them there, was it the Igman Brigade or the Ilidza Brigade, and it appears you answered: "The Igman brigade?" Was that a question or were you making -- affirmatively answering that it was the Igman Brigade who was keeping them there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me and I answered. The Igman Brigade. Commander Cojic kept them there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So moving onto the Markale market massacre. Now, you weren't involved in any of the investigations whatsoever into this incident, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. It wasn't my right to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you haven't read any of the investigative reports on the incident?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I didn't read any of the reports, but I heard two different versions of the reports from two different sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, at the time of the meeting, would you say that foreign observers were viewed suspiciously by the VRS? By 1994.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the VRS. Everybody was suspicious of the foreign military observers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So Colonel Marko Lugonja, you refer to him as having been at this meeting, and you referred to him generally as Galic's security guy. Can you tell us what position he held?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mentioned Colonel Lugonja, he was in charge of intelligence. When we say a security guy, we mean somebody who is in charge of intelligence and security, and he was the number one man in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps when it came to intelligence, security, and obviously the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And so this is the Colonel Marko Lugonja who is the subordinate of Colonel Ljubisa Beara, Colonels Petar Salapura, and General Tolimir. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he was subordinate to Ljubisa Beara and I don't know about the other two generals; i.e., whether Lugonja was subordinate to them as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, you really have no opinion about what happened at Markale, which you've told us. So all you're telling us is that the chief of intelligence and security of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps a few hours after this massacre happens meets with foreign observers, who he is suspicious of, and tells them that this is a staged event, that the Muslims are planting bodies there, that it's a big plot, a big conspiracy involving civilians, the army, the hospital. This is what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: When you say that he was suspicious of military observers, I say with full responsibility that we were very good friends Jan [phoen] who was with me there, so we cannot generalise. It is true that Mr. Lugonja was an intelligence man. But I claim with full responsibility that the first meeting with Lugonja in front of Hotel Serbia, I know as an interpreter when people lie, I am claiming that Lugonja was shocked with that incident. These are the powers that I've acquired while interpreting for such a long number of years. I know exactly when somebody is lying and when somebody is telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then you're better off than many in this world who sometimes need some time to find out whether somebody is telling the truth or not. But could you please answer the question. The question is whether your evidence is limited to what you heard Lugonja say two hours after the event, and then Ms. Hasan repeated some of what you said you had heard. That is your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can repeat what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I don't like it when words are put into my mouth or when some things are generalised. Like, for example, when it was said that we were all suspicious of all the military observers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you gave it a more general meeting by saying not only the VRS but everyone. So if there's anyone responsible for making that a broad statement, then it's you yourself, Mr. Batinic. But that was the previous question. I asked you to answer this question. That is, whether the evidence you give to us is what you heard Lugonja say about Markale. That's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing more, nothing less. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, you testified yesterday at transcript page 22622, lines 13 to 23, that you were both an interpreter for your commander and for the UNMOs. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the year 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, you can tell me.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday I said that the Commander Blagota Kovacevic said: "From now on, you will be my interpreter." I thought I was only his interpreter, but I carried a UN card so I was confused myself. It was only in July 1993 that I took off my uniform and I started working already on the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, there may be some confusion about the page number. Because in my system, but I noticed before that sometimes there's a slight difference, it is page 22621 where, on those lines, this information is found. Please proceed. But it's just to avoid that others are not finding it later on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, Witness, when you changed out of your uniform, once you were authorised to take off your uniform, you were still a member of the Igman Brigade, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether I was a member of the Igman Brigade. From then on I never put on a uniform, nor did anybody tell me that I was no longer a member of the Igman Brigade. I wore civilian clothes and I served as an interpreter for UN observers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: From whom were you receiving a salary in 1993? In 1992, tell us first. And then in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received my first and last salaries from the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry, your first and last salaries, meaning in 1992 you received a salary from the -- from the UN. 1993, you received a salary from the UN. 1994? Okay. Did you receive any salary from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was some sort of salary in dinars. I believe that the amount was some 20 German marks. I never took it. Actually, I gave it to my neighbour. I did not want to have anything to do with that money, with that salary.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
